deep.reconstruction:
This folio has no mathematics. It is the opening of a later fair copy ('Abschrift') of a letter, and the pencil note says the original is in Gauss's Nachlass. The visible text is: archival label 'Riemann 2'; pencil note '(Original im Nachl. Gauss!)'; heading 'Abschrift.'; salutation 'Ew. Hochwohlgeboren'; and the first lines 'bitte ich um gütige Nachsicht, wenn ich Sie noch einmal belästige wegen der Frage über die Möglichkeit der Transformation des Aus-'. The sentence continues on the next page with 'drucks Ω = p dx + p' dx' + ... + p^(n-1) dx^(n-1)'.

The faint writing in the background is bleed-through or offset from the next page. It shows the system (A) with the bracket coefficients (μ,ν) = ∂p^(μ)/∂x^(ν) − ∂p^(ν)/∂x^(μ) and the footnote identity; none of it is new content on this page.

Context: Riemann is writing to Gauss a second time ('noch einmal') about the Pfaff problem. The question is when a Pfaffian form in n variables can be brought, up to a common factor e^t, to a form in one fewer variable. On the next page he apologises for having first overlooked that Gauss's remark in the Göttingische gelehrte Anzeigen (1815, p. 1035) is correct for Pfaff's original equations. He explains that he had met the remark in a paper of Jacobi, where it is applied to the derived equations, for which it no longer holds. The previous folio (91v) is the end of a different letter, in Italian, signed by Riemann; it concerns the attraction or potential of an ellipsoid.

results.what: Opening of a (copied) letter from Riemann to Gauss on reducing a Pfaffian expression Ω = Σ p^(i) dx^(i) to one with one fewer variable, up to a factor e^t. Only the salutation and the statement of topic are on this page.
results.modern_name: Pfaff problem (normal forms of Pfaffian forms / differential 1-forms)
results.usually_credited_to: J. F. Pfaff (1815); C. G. J. Jacobi (1827); later Grassmann, Clebsch, Frobenius (1877), Darboux (1882)

deep.surprise_reason: This page holds only the salutation and the first line of a letter stating its topic, with no mathematics. That Riemann corresponded with Gauss about the Pfaff problem is itself a modest archival detail. Any mathematical content is on the following pages.
